Chapter 6: The Stories We Tell Ourselves.
You know, we all carry around a collection of stories—narratives we tell ourselves about who we are, what we’re capable of, and how the world works. These stories aren’t just random—they’ve been shaped by our experiences, by what we’ve picked up from our culture, and by what others expect from us.
Sometimes, these stories lift us up. They give us a sense of purpose, and open up possibilities we might not have seen otherwise. But other times, those same stories can hold us back. They keep us stuck in roles that no longer fit, or make us doubt what we’re truly capable of.
Let me give you an example. Imagine someone who’s always struggled with public speaking. For years, they believed they were just “not a confident person.” That story probably started way back in childhood—maybe there was a moment when they froze up in front of the class, and that memory just stuck. Over time, the story kept playing in their mind, shaping their choices and fueling self-doubt.
But here’s where it gets interesting. One day, a supportive colleague encouraged them to give it another shot, but in a really low-pressure setting. The first attempt? Honestly, it was shaky. But the world didn’t end. And with each small success, that old narrative started to lose its grip.
Here’s another example. Maybe you grew up hearing, “money doesn’t grow on trees.” For someone, that story might’ve been passed down for generations, creating a sense of scarcity that lingers well into adulthood. Even when things get better, that old fear of not having enough can hang around. It takes real effort to notice when that belief is influencing your decisions, and to gently challenge it. Over time, experimenting with new ways of thinking about abundance and security can make all the difference.
Most of us don’t realize just how much these internal stories shape our lives. They guide our relationships, our career choices—even our health. But the best part? These stories aren’t set in stone. You can rewrite them.
It all starts with noticing the narrative. Ask yourself—where did this story come from? Is it even true anymore? Sometimes, just sharing your story with a trusted friend or a therapist can loosen its hold. And step by step, new stories can start to take root—ones that reflect your growth, your resilience, and all the possibilities ahead.
